You found a Bitcoin backup. Take your time.

Nothing here is urgent. Bitcoin does not expire, and nobody can take it while the backup stays private. Go slowly, one step at a time, and do not let anyone rush you. This page works offline and sends nothing anywhere.

  1. Keep it private. Do not type the words into a website, an app or a phone, and do not photograph them. Never give them to anyone: no real company, exchange, lawyer or support person ever needs them. Anyone who asks for them, or offers to recover the money for a fee, is a thief.
  2. What do you have?
    • 12 or 24 words (sometimes 15, 18 or 21): a seed phrase, also called a recovery phrase. The words are the wallet.
    • Words plus another word or sentence, called a passphrase or 25th word: both are needed, exactly as written (capital letters and spaces count).
    • A metal plate or cards with words or their first letters: the same words, stamped so they survive fire and water.
    • A small device (Trezor, Ledger, Coldcard, BitBox, Jade and others): a hardware wallet. It needs its PIN; the words written for it open the wallet without the device.
    • Several sets of words, or a note like “2 of 3” or “multisig”: a multisig wallet. It needs more than one set of words plus the wallet’s setup file (a descriptor). Set up a multisig wallet, in EXTRA TOOLS, explains it.
    • A long code starting with xpub, ypub or zpub: a watch-only key. It shows the balance but cannot spend.
    • A code starting with bc1, 1 or 3: an address. It shows where money was received; it cannot spend.
    • A code that starts with 5, K or L, or with xprv: a private key, as on an old paper wallet. Treat it like the words.
    • A VOIDFORGE BACKUP PLAN sheet: it says where the copies are, what wallet app was used and who can help. It holds no words.
  3. Check that the words are complete and right. VERIFY says whether they make a valid backup, and its fingerprint is the wallet’s name tag. If a word is missing, wrong or hard to read, Reforge (in EXTRA TOOLS) can often find it.
  4. Find the wallet. If the right words open an empty wallet, the app may be looking in the wrong place. If you know one address the wallet used (from old emails, statements or exchange withdrawals), the Wallet Detective finds which app made it and how to open it.
  5. See the balance without risk. After VERIFY, Open this wallet lists the wallet’s addresses, 10 at a time. Compare them with old statements or exchange withdrawals, or look one up in a block explorer on another device: it shows the balance, and the words never touch an online device.
  6. Move the money only when you are ready (and, for an inheritance, after legal advice). Install a well-known wallet app from its own website, or use a hardware wallet, restore the words there, send a small test amount first, and keep the words private until everything is moved.
Scam warnings.
  • Nobody genuine will ever ask for the words, the passphrase or a photo of them.
  • “Recovery services” and “support agents” who contact you first are thieves, however official they look.
  • Fake wallet apps copy real names. Install apps only from the maker’s own website, never from a link someone sent you.
  • Never type the words into a website, even one that says it checks them.
  • Ask people you already trust for help, not people who found you. An estate lawyer needs to know the wallet exists, never the words.

MAKE A SEED

Pick 12 or 24 words, enter your dice rolls or coin flips, then press FORGE SEED and write the words on paper.

Step 1 of 5

Choose how your seed is made

Your wallet starts as a very large random number. Real dice (or a coin) are how you create it yourself, instead of trusting a computer to pick it. First choose the length: 12 words is strong enough for almost everyone and needs about 50 dice rolls. 24 words is the longest option and needs about 99 rolls. Then choose dice (easier for most people) or coin (many more flips). If you have physical word tiles, use the Word draw box instead. Making real keys? First read “Before you make real keys” (the Read before real keys link near the top of the page).

Roll your dice

Roll a real die, then tap the number it shows. Do not make numbers up: people are bad at being random, and the whole point is that nobody could guess your rolls. You need at least 50 rolls; more are fine, and every one counts. The bar fills as you go, and NEXT unlocks when you have enough. The gray words below change with every roll, so you can see how one roll changes every word. Make sure nobody can see your screen.

Forge the seed and write it down

Press FORGE SEED. Your rolls are scrambled together into your seed words. (A passphrase, if you want one, comes next, after you can see the words.) Write the words on paper, in order, with a pen. Never take a photo, type them into a connected device, or store them in a cloud. Anyone who has these words has your money. NEXT unlocks once the words are shown.

Optional: add a passphrase

A passphrase is an extra secret that makes a different wallet from the same words. It protects you if someone finds your paper, but if you lose it the funds are gone for good. If you are not sure, skip this step. If you want one, type it twice in the Passphrase box under your words. The page then shows the fingerprint without the passphrase and with it, so you can see they are different wallets. Write the passphrase down separately from the words.

Check it and make a backup

Last step, and the most important. Compare the fingerprint and first address in a second wallet app, make a paper backup if you like (SeedQR or the printed sheet), then press START DRILL in the Restore drill below: it hides the words on screen and has you type them back from your paper. (The CHECK A BACKUP tab can also check words you already have.) Start with a small amount first.

Word draw: made your words with physical tiles?SECRETType words drawn from word tiles (such as SeedSigner’s SeedPills) or picked with dice (such as BitBox02’s diceware table), plus a few coin flips.
How Word draw works

Word tiles let you pick the words by hand: mix them in a bag, draw one without looking, flip it to choose a face, write the word down and put the tile back before the next draw. Each word is 11 random bits. A 12-word seed needs 11 drawn words and 7 coin flips; a 24-word seed needs 23 words and 3 flips. The flips are needed because part of the last word is a checksum. Type your words (the first four letters of each are enough) and your flips; VOIDFORGE finishes the last word the standard BIP39 way, with no hashing, so any BIP39 wallet reads the result. Repeated words are fine, because every draw goes back in the bag. It never fills in the flips for you. Typed words are secret: use it only where nobody can see your screen.

Using dice instead of tiles?
Type a word number (1–2048), or a D8 roll followed by two 16-sided dice (0–F), written with a space between them, such as 3 A 7 (a plain number with no spaces is a word number). The word number is (D8 − 1) × 256 + the two hex digits + 1. For the final word of a 24-word seed, a last D8 roll gives 3 bits: write it as flips (1 = 000, 2 = 001 ... 8 = 111).
Using BitBox02’s diceware table?
BitBox02 diceware makes a 24-word seed. For each of the first 23 words, roll four dice, then a fifth, re-rolling any 5 or 6 so every die shows 1 to 4, and flip a coin. Type them like 2143 2 T (the four dice, the fifth die, H or T) and press ADD WORD or Enter: you get the same word as BitBox’s printed table. For the last word, BitBox shows 8 choices and you flip 3 coins (HHH picks the first, TTT the eighth). Type those 3 flips in the flips box below with T as 1 and H as 0 (HHT is 001), and the page makes the same 24th word BitBox would.
The passphrase (if any) is added after the words are made, in the box under them. Coin: pick which side is 1 and keep it the same for every flip (for BitBox02’s last word, T is 1 and H is 0).
Cards and hexSECRET
How cards work

Use a full deck of 52 cards with the jokers taken out. Shuffle it well (at least seven riffle shuffles), lay the cards out face up and type them in order, such as AS 10H QD 2C: the rank (A, 2 to 10, J, Q, K) and then the suit (C, D, H or S; ♠ ♥ ♦ ♣ work too). A 12-word seed needs 25 cards. A 24-word seed needs the whole deck and then 6 more from a new shuffle. VOIDFORGE writes the cards as A♠ 2♣ T♦ and so on and hashes that text with SHA-256, as Ian Coleman’s BIP39 tool does (choose Cards and the number of words there, not raw entropy, and type T for a 10) and EntropyLab’s Coleman symbols option, so you can check the words with either.

Or hex: a 16-sided die, or checking another tool

Type exactly 32 hex digits (0 to 9 and a to f) for 12 words, or 64 for 24 words. They are used directly as the seed’s randomness, with no hashing, as in Ian Coleman’s tool with Hexadecimal and raw entropy chosen. For a real seed, roll a 16-sided die yourself (one digit per roll). Never use hex that a website or a program made for you.

The passphrase (if any) is added after the words are made, in the box under them.
DICE TEST ONLY: no seed is made from these rolls. Turn the test off in “Your rolls” below to make a seed.
Pick which side is 1 and which is 0 (the usual choice: heads = 1, tails = 0) and keep it the same for every flip. Only the 1/0 string is used, so any consistent choice is fine, but you cannot get the mapping back from the words. Write down the exact string or your mapping with your backup.
0 / 50 rolls
Your rolls: history and fairness chartSee what you rolled and whether the faces came up evenly, or test your dice without making a seed.
Roll together (two people or two dice)
Two or more people, or two or more dice, can make one seed together: each rolls with their own die, and all the rolls go into the roll box, in turn. Every roll is hashed together, but hashing only mixes the rolls; it cannot add randomness. So let each die roll the full count on its own (50 for 12 words, 99 for 24): for example 50 rolls with one die, then 50 with the other, 100 in all, and FORGE hashes every one. Then the words are random as long as one of the dice is fair and rolled honestly: a loaded die, or someone who picks numbers instead of rolling, cannot make the seed predictable. Using dice from two different shops protects you from one bad die. Everyone who sees all the rolls can make the seed again, so roll together only with people you would trust with the seed itself, and keep the rolls as secret as the words.
YOUR SEED
SECRET These words are your money. Write them on paper and never share them.
—
Passphrase and note (optional)
About passphrases
A passphrase makes a different wallet from the same words. Write it down separately: without it the funds cannot be recovered. Some hardware wallets limit how long a passphrase can be or which characters it can use, so test a small amount on your device before you rely on it.
Make a passphrase from dice
Roll a die again, separately from the rolls for your seed, and these new rolls become a passphrase of BIP39 words. They are hashed with SHA-256, as for the seed, and each word takes the next 11 bits. Keep the passphrase apart from the seed words: anyone with both can spend, and the words alone open a different wallet. Choose 6 or 8 words: fewer could be searched by someone who has your seed words.

      Paper backup as a SeedQRSECRETFor SeedSigner and similar offline devices. Print it or copy it by hand.
      
          A SeedQR is your seed words as a QR code, so anyone who can scan it controls the funds: treat it exactly like the written words. Scan it only with an offline device such as a SeedSigner, never with a phone camera app. It does not contain the passphrase. SeedQR is the digit format (25×25 squares for 12 words, 29×29 for 24). CompactSeedQR is smaller (21×21 or 25×25). SeedSigner reads both.

              Tamper-evident bags
              
      
              A tamper-evident bag shows when it has been opened, and each bag has its own serial number. Seal each copy of the words in its own bag. Write down the serial (or photograph the sealed bag, never the words) and keep that record apart from the bag. At each check-up (the 5-minute routine on the printed plan), first check that the seal is intact and that the serial matches your record. A changed serial or a broken seal means: assume the backup was seen, and move the money to a new wallet. If you open a bag yourself to read the words, seal them in a new bag and write down its serial. PRINT BAG LOG prints a sheet for all of this.

                Explain an address, or check that it is yours
                
      
                Paste any Bitcoin address and VOIDFORGE explains it at once: what kind it is, which network, whether it has a typo, and what someone can do with it. That needs no seed. To find it in your wallet, paste a receive or change address from a wallet app (bc1q SegWit, bc1p Taproot, 3 nested SegWit or 1 legacy; the box on the right is the account, almost always 0). It is searched in the wallet made by the words and passphrase above.
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
        Check an address before you payCompare every character of the address you are about to pay with the one you were given.
        
                Two common scams make a look-alike address whose first and last characters match the real one: a tiny payment from it lands in your history so you copy it by mistake later, or malware swaps the address you copied. Checking only the ends does not catch either. Paste the address from your wallet’s send screen, then the one the person gave you (from their message, invoice or QR code). Nothing is sent anywhere.
                
        
        
        
                
        
                
      
                
      
                
      
                Not sure of the account? TRY ACCOUNTS 0 TO 20 looks at the first 20 receive and change addresses of each account (the account box is ignored), with and without the passphrase above. It takes a while; STOP ends it.
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      
                My wallet shows zero: Wallet DetectiveUSES THE WORDS ABOVE
                
      
                When the right words open an empty wallet, the app is often looking in a different place: another address type, account or path, a passphrase, or an Electrum seed. Type the words (and the passphrase, if any) in the boxes at the top of this tab, then one address you know this wallet received to (from an old message, invoice or exchange withdrawal). FIND MY WALLET tries the settings of well-known wallet apps until that address matches, then names the apps that use them and how to open it. It never looks up a balance. A search can take a minute or two (longer with a passphrase); STOP ends it. No address? LIST FIRST ADDRESSES shows the first address of each common setting, to look up on another device.
                
      
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      
                Is this seed in my wallet file?USES THE WORDS ABOVE
                
      
                For a multisig wallet (or any wallet with a descriptor): paste its setup file, the output descriptor, the Coldcard multisig setup file or the BSMS record (or choose the file), with the seed words (and passphrase, if any) typed in the boxes above. VOIDFORGE checks every key in the file: is it made by this seed, with the fingerprint, path and key all matching? So you know which key of the wallet this backup is, before you rely on it. The file holds only public keys.
                
      
      
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      
                Read a label file (BIP329)PRIVATE
                
      
                Wallet apps such as Sparrow, Bitcoin Core and Nunchuk can export their labels (“Rent, March”, “Savings”) as a BIP329 file. Paste it or choose it: VOIDFORGE lists every label and, with the seed words typed above, says which labeled addresses are this seed’s (the first 100 receive and change addresses of each address type, account 0). Labels are private: they link coins to you. The file is only read here, never stored or sent.
                
      
      
      
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
  
                
  
                

  
                
  
                
    
                EXTRA TOOLS
                
    
                Optional helpers. They only display; none of them can spend or sign.
                
    
                
      Reforge: recover a seed or find a passphraseSECRETMissing or wrong words, or a forgotten passphrase — search against what you already know.
      
                Reforge searches for the words or passphrase you lost, checked against something you know is right: your wallet’s master fingerprint, one of its addresses, or its account xpub/zpub (all three are public, and a watch-only wallet shows them). It never guesses: it reports only what matched, and tells you plainly when nothing did. What you type here is secret; it is never saved or sent, and CLEAR wipes it.
                
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
                
        
                Type your words in order, with ? for each word you do not have. Reforge picks the search from what you type: with one or two ? it tries every word in those places; with all the words it tries every swap of two words and every single word replaced; with one word fewer (11, 14, 17, 20 or 23) it tries the missing word at every place. A word that is not on the BIP39 list counts as ?, and the first 4 letters of a word are enough. To list the words that could be last, type all but the last word, then ?. Two ? on a 12-word phrase can take a long time; an account xpub/zpub is by far the fastest thing to check against (a fingerprint or an address is several times slower), the page shows progress, and STOP ends the search.
                
        
        
        
        
                
          
          
          
        
                
      
                
      
                
        
                For a wallet whose words you have but whose passphrase you do not remember exactly. Type your seed words, then your guesses or the pieces you remember, one per line, exactly as you might have typed them (spaces count). Reforge tries no passphrase, each line, and every two or three lines joined (with or without a space, in any order), each as typed, in lowercase, in UPPERCASE and Capitalised; tick one typo to also try each with a character missing, doubled, swapped with the next one, or in the other case. Each try takes the browser about a millisecond against an xpub/zpub and several times longer against a fingerprint or address, so the page counts the tries first and refuses more than 1,000,000.
                
        
        
        
        
        
                
          
          
          
        
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Check your device's diceTEST ONLYDoes your hardware wallet really make its words from your dice? Check it with throwaway rolls.
      
                A hardware wallet that takes dice rolls should make its words from them alone. If its software ignored your rolls, the words would still look normal. So check it once: type the same throwaway rolls here and on the device, and the words must be the same. Then reset the device before making your real wallet, because test rolls and their words are not secret.
                
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
      
                0 / 50 rolls (exactly 50 for SeedSigner)
                
      
                
        
        
        
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Inspect a transaction (PSBT)READ ONLYSee where the money goes and the fee before signing.
      
                Shows what a partly signed Bitcoin transaction (PSBT) from a wallet app would do: where the money comes from, where it goes, and the fee, so you can check it before signing on your hardware wallet. This only reads and displays. It cannot sign, never uses your seed words, and sends nothing. Paste the PSBT (base64 or hex) or choose the .psbt file. If you typed your words in the CHECK A BACKUP tab, outputs that carry this wallet’s key information are marked. It also checks any signatures it finds: whether two of them share a nonce (a repeated secret number that lets anyone work out the private key) and whether a signature covers the whole transaction.
                
      
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Compare two transactionsREAD ONLYDid the signer change anything? Is a fee bump a plain fee bump?
      
                Paste the transaction you sent and the one that came back (from your signer or wallet). Or paste an original and its fee-bump replacement. This lists every difference in plain words. It only reads and compares. It cannot sign and sends nothing anywhere.
                
      
      
      
      
      
                
        
        
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      What will spending cost later?NO KEYS NEEDEDHow the number of deposits and the address type change the fee to spend them.
      
                Every deposit you receive becomes a separate coin, and spending pays a fee for each coin used. Many small deposits can cost more to spend than they are worth when fees are high. This works out the size of a payment that spends them all, and its fee at a few fee rates. It is arithmetic only: no network, no prices, sats only.
                
      
                
        
        
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Verify a signed messageREAD ONLYCheck that the key of an address signed a message. This page never signs.
      
                Paste the address, the message exactly as it was signed, and the signature from the wallet that made it. Two formats are checked: the classic one (BIP137, from Bitcoin Core, Electrum, Sparrow, Trezor, Coldcard and others, for 1..., 3... and bc1q... addresses) and BIP322 “simple” signatures for single-key bc1q... and bc1p... addresses. A whole signed-message block (BEGIN BITCOIN SIGNED MESSAGE) can go in the message box. It only checks. It cannot sign and sends nothing. Every character of the message counts, including spaces and line breaks.
                
      
      
      
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Seed XOR: split or combineSECRETSplit one seed into 2 to 4 parts that are all needed, or combine parts, as Coldcard does.
      
                Seed XOR (made by Coldcard) turns one 12, 18 or 24-word seed into 2, 3 or 4 parts. Each part is itself a normal-looking seed phrase that opens an empty wallet, so a thief who finds one part learns nothing. To get the seed back you need every part: lose one and the money is lost. That is the opposite of multisig, where some keys may be lost; if you want to survive a lost backup, use a 2-of-3 multisig instead. The passphrase, if any, is not split: it stays with the combined seed.
                
      
                
        
        
      
                
      
                
        
                Splits the words typed at the top of CHECK A BACKUP. As with the seed, the randomness comes from your dice: roll again (at least 50 times for 12 words, 75 for 18, 99 for 24) and type the results. Or choose the same parts a Coldcard makes for this seed: no rolls needed, but anyone who holds the seed can make those parts again (and can tell the parts came from it).
                
        
                
          
          
        
                
        
        
                
      
                
      
                
        
        
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      SLIP39 shares (Shamir backup)SECRETCheck SLIP39 shares, or combine them to see which wallet they open.
      
                A SLIP39 backup (a Shamir backup, made by Trezor and Keystone) is a set of shares of 20 or 33 words each, from a list of 1,024 words that is not the BIP39 list. A set number of them (for example 2 of 3) opens the wallet; fewer reveal nothing. Type each share on its own line. VOIDFORGE checks every share, and with enough of them shows the wallet’s master fingerprint and first addresses, so you can compare them with your device. It only reads shares; it never makes them. Do this only on your offline computer.
                
      
      
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Child seed (BIP85)SECRETMake a separate new seed, key or password from this one.
      
                Makes a brand new seed phrase from the parent words (and passphrase) typed in the CHECK A BACKUP tab, for a separate wallet, using the BIP85 standard. BIP85 can also make a Bitcoin Core HD seed (WIF), a master xprv, hex bytes, a password (Base64 or Base85) or dice rolls: choose one under “What to make”. The same parent, type, settings and index always give the same result. The child is as secret as the parent. It is shown here, with no copy or save; its print button prints it on one sheet, after asking, for a trusted offline printer only. Use the same safety steps as for a new seed, and keep the parent safe: if you lose the parent you lose every child.
                
      
                
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
    
                
      Check your downloadPick the VOIDFORGE file you downloaded and compare its fingerprint with the published one.
      
                Choose the voidforge.html file you downloaded. The page works out its SHA-256 hash and its content ID (CID) here on your computer, then compares them with the values from the release page (paste the hash, the CID, or a whole line of SHA256SUMS). The file is only read: it is not stored, changed or sent anywhere.
                
      
                Know the limit: a page cannot vouch for itself. A tampered copy could lie to you here, so for real money also run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS with a tool that is not this page (RELEASING.md shows how). A copy saved with DOWNLOAD FOR USB is a re-saved page and will not match the release file.
                
      
      
      
                
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
      
                Check a signed release (as Sparrow Wallet checks its downloads). Pick the three files from the release page together: voidforge.html, SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.asc. The page checks the GPG signature on SHA256SUMS with the VOIDFORGE signing key built into it, fingerprint 2509 D115 03B7 2CBF BCB5  408F 4B72 9F05 6A52 9340, then checks that voidforge.html is the file SHA256SUMS lists. Releases from v2.8.1 on are signed. The files are only read: nothing is stored or sent.
                
      
                Know the limit: the key and the check are inside this page, so a tampered page could fake both. The first time, check the download with GnuPG (RELEASING.md shows how); after that, a copy you have checked can check new downloads. Compare the fingerprint above with the one in SECURITY.md and on the project page.
                
      
      
                
        
      
                
      
                
      
                
      
                
    
                
  
                

  
                
    
                MULTISIG WALLETNEW
                
    
                Share control of your coins between several keys, so that no single lost or stolen key can empty the wallet.
                
    
                
      Set up a multisig walletGuided, one key at a time. Seeds are wiped from this page after each key.
      
                
        
                
          
                What it is. A multisig wallet is built from N keys and spends only when M of them agree. With 2-of-3, losing one key loses nothing, and a thief with one key gets nothing.
                
          
                What it costs. More to back up, and setup takes longer. Every key is its own seed with its own paper backup, kept in a different place.
                
          
                How this works. You make one key at a time. After each, the seed is wiped from the page and only the public key is kept.
                
        
                
        
                2-of-32 keys needed to spend, out of 3 total
                
        
                
          
          
        
                
        
                
          
                
          
          
        
                
        
                
        
                keys needed to spend (M)total keys (N)
                
        
                Popular: 
                
        
                
        
                
          
          
          
        
                
        
                
        
                
      
                
      
                
        
                
        
                
        
                TESTNET (practice coins only). These keys and addresses are not for real money.
                
        
                
        
                
          
                Paste the public key of another signer: a Zpub/xpub, or the whole [fingerprint/48h/...]xpub... line from their device. Never paste a private key or seed words here.
                
          
          
                
          
                
        
                
        
                
        
                
          
                ✓Your multisig wallet is ready
                
          
                All keys were made on this one device. That is convenient, but it puts every key in one place for a while: anyone who could read this device’s memory during setup could get all of them. For real protection, make each key on a different device (or at least after a restart), store each backup in a different place, and use the paste option above to combine only the public keys.
                
          
                
          
                Descriptor (public, safe to keep): import it in Sparrow, Nunchuk or Bitcoin Core
                
          
                
          
                
          
                
            
                
            
                
            
          
                
          
                Animated QR for a signing device or wallet app
                
          
                No one QR format reaches every device, so pick yours. Each is the same wallet, public keys only.
                
          
                
          
                
            
                
            
                
            
                
            
                
          
                
          
                
          
                
          
                Change descriptor (only if your app asks for it separately)
                
          
                
          
          
                
          
                
          
                First 10 receive addresses: after importing, your app must show exactly these
                
          
                  
          
                  First 10 change addresses
                  
          
                    
          
                    
          
                    The descriptor contains only public keys. It lets a wallet app watch the balance and make receiving addresses; it cannot spend. To spend you need M of the seeds, so keep every seed backup safe, and keep a copy of this descriptor (the recovery sheet) with them: without it, the seeds alone are not enough to find the funds.
                    
        
                    
        
                    
        
                    Honest note: after you press ADD, the seed is erased from the page, but a browser cannot promise it also erased every trace from memory. For the strictest safety, reload or restart before the next key, or make the next key on another device and paste its public key.
                    
      
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Check descriptors for a reused keyPUBLIC KEYS ONLYCatches the same key, or the same seed, used twice in a wallet or a multisig setup.
      
                    Paste one or more output descriptors (one per line), for example the multisig descriptor from your wallet app and the single-key descriptors you also use. VOIDFORGE lists every public key in them and warns when a key appears twice, when two keys of one multisig come from the same seed, or when the same fingerprint and path give different keys. Private keys are refused.
                    
      
      
                    
      
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Find a typo in a descriptorPUBLIC KEYS ONLYA descriptor that will not import, or a checksum that does not match: which character is wrong.
      
                    Paste the descriptor exactly as it was written down or copied, with its checksum (the 8 characters after #). One wrong character always changes the checksum, so VOIDFORGE tries every single change (a character replaced, two neighbors swapped, one left out or added) and shows the one that makes the descriptor match its checksum again, with every key valid. It only reads public keys; it cannot spend.
                    
      
      
                    
      
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Explain an inheritance or timelock walletPUBLIC KEYS ONLYWho can spend, and from when: Liana, Nunchuk and other miniscript wallets in plain words.
      
                    Inheritance and recovery wallets (Liana, Nunchuk’s timelocked wallets, Bitcoin Core) are described by a descriptor with conditions such as older(52560). Paste it here: VOIDFORGE lists every way the coins can be spent, which keys must sign, and how long each one has to wait. With the seed words typed in CHECK A BACKUP, it also says which key those words are. Type the current block height (any block explorer, or your wallet app, shows it) to turn a fixed block into a rough date. It only reads public keys; it cannot spend.
                    
      
      
      
                    
      
                    
    
                    
  
                    
  
                    

  
                    
  
                    
    AIR-GAPPED USE ONLY for real funds.
                    
    Never enter a real seed on a connected device.
                    
    Always verify with a second offline tool before trusting real Bitcoin.
    
                    VOIDFORGE is an educational tool and has not been independently audited. Provided as is, without warranty. You alone are responsible for your funds and backups. Lost words or passphrase mean lost funds. Test the backup and start with a small amount.
                    
  
                    

  
                    ⚠ BEFORE YOU MAKE REAL KEYS
                    

                    Three ways a computer can quietly keep your secrets, and the simple fix for each.
                    

                    1
                    Your computer may keep a copy of your keys. It can write memory to the hard drive (swap files, hibernation) without asking, and the browser cannot stop it.What to do: for real money, use an offline computer with an encrypted drive, and turn hibernation off.
                    

                    2
                    Copying can leak. Clipboard history can keep what you copy or paste, and may sync it to your other devices.What to do: write seeds on paper; avoid copy and paste for anything secret, and turn clipboard history off.
                    

                    3
                    Keys can stay in memory after you finish. Wiping the page is a precaution, not a guarantee.What to do: when you are done, close the browser and restart the computer.
                    

  
                    
    
                    IS ANYTHING WATCHING THIS PAGE?
                    
    
                    Browser extensions (password managers, writing assistants, translators, wallet extensions) and other software can read a page and everything typed into it, including seed words. This looks for the signs they leave on this page: scripts, frames and elements it never makes, attributes it never sets, translation, objects that wallet extensions add, a frame around the page, and automation. It checks by itself as the page runs and shows a warning at the top when it finds one. It can only find signs, so it never says the page is safe.
                    
    
                    
    
                    
    
                    
  
                    

  
                    
    
                    ABOUT & HELP
                    
    
                    VOIDFORGE is an educational tool. It is open source, works fully offline and is meant to be read, but it has not been independently audited. Use it to learn and to make keys you understand, practice first, and start real money with a small amount.
                    
    
                    
      How to use
      
                      
        
                    1. Copy this single file to a USB stick and open it on an air-gapped computer.
                      2. 
        
                    2. Press SELF-TEST and confirm it says all tests passed.
                      3. 
        
                    3. Choose Dice or Coin (or Word draw if you drew physical word tiles), enter your physical rolls or flips, and press FORGE SEED. For coins, decide which side is 1 and which is 0 (heads = 1, tails = 0 is the usual choice), use it for every flip, and record the exact 1/0 string with your backup. You can type, paste, or tap the buttons above the box.
                      4. 
        
                    4. Compare the words and the master fingerprint with a second independent offline tool before trusting real funds.
                      5. 
        
                    5. To check a backup later, type the words into VERIFY, add the passphrase if you used one, and paste the fingerprint or first address you wrote down into the last box. VERIFY tells you whether it matches without a passphrase, with it, or neither.
                      6.

It is built into the page, works offline and stores nothing. It is updated with every release, and where a word appears in VOIDFORGE the entry says where.

      Browser safety checklistEight quick habits that keep your seed on the page and nowhere else.
      
                    This page works offline, but the browser and computer around it can still keep copies of what you see. None of these steps is hard, and each one closes a real gap.
                    
      
                      
        
                    1. Go offline first. Turn off Wi-Fi and unplug the network cable before you open the page. The “WARNING: this computer looks ONLINE” banner is only a hint, so do not rely on it.
                      2. 
        
                    2. For real funds, open the file from a USB stick or a local folder on an offline computer, never from a website. Check the file’s SHA256 first (see the README). The online copy on the project page is for practice only. Its address is random21m.gitlab.io/voidforge, the only link on this page; it opens in a new tab, and your browser contacts that site only if you click it.
                      3. 
        
                    3. Use a fresh browser window with extensions turned off. A private window is not enough: extensions can still read every page.
                      4. 
        
                    4. Turn off page translation, read-aloud and screen sharing. Translation tools may send the page text, including your words, to a server.
                      5. 
        
                    5. Mind the clipboard. Copying seed words or a SeedQR can leave them in clipboard history, and some systems sync that history. Clear it afterwards, or write by hand instead of copying.
                      6. 
        
                    6. Printing and “save as PDF” make files. Delete them and check the printer queue afterwards. A printer that is not on a network is best.
                      7. 
        
                    7. Check the Downloads folder and any auto-saved files when you are done, and delete anything you made.
                      8. 
        
                    8. Finish by closing the page, then restart the browser or, better, the computer. That clears what the page left in memory.
                      9. 
      
                    
      
                    A browser is not a hardware wallet. This checklist lowers the risk; it does not remove it, which is why we also ask you to test with a small amount first.
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Privacy: what this page does with your dataWhat it keeps, what it never sends, and the only ways anything leaves.
      
                      
        
                    • Nothing is sent anywhere. The page has no code that talks to the internet, and a rule built into the file (a Content-Security-Policy) tells the browser to block all network access as a second line of defense. You can read the file to check; there is no server, no account and no tracking.
                      • 
        
                    • Only two things are remembered between visits: your light or dark choice and your text size, in your browser’s local storage. Your rolls, flips, words, passphrase and fingerprint are never stored. Close the page and they are gone from the page.
                      • 
        
                    • One note for this tab only: while the computer is offline, closing the start notice puts a single “1” in this tab’s session storage, so the notice does not come back every time you reload. It lasts only as long as the tab, and END SESSION (MENU) deletes it straight away. Nothing else goes there, and nothing at all while the computer is online.
                      • 
        
                    • Your secrets live only in the page’s memory while it is open. The WIPE button and closing the tab clear them from the page, but not from anything your computer copied in the meantime (see the safety checklist above).
                      • 
        
                    • Things leave the page only when you press a button for them: COPY (to your clipboard), PRINT, and DOWNLOAD. Each one makes a copy outside the page, so each is your call.
                      • 
        
                    • Secret and public are labeled. Words, the passphrase and SeedQR are secret. The fingerprint, addresses, watch-only export and multisig descriptor are public data, safe to show a second computer, though they let others see your balance.
                      • 
        
                    • The practice phrase is not a real seed. It is one of the published BIP39 test phrases, used only to practice writing words down. The page makes no random numbers of its own.
                      • 
      
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      How multisig works, and what it costsSeveral keys, any M of them can spend. Read this before you set one up.
      
                    A multisig wallet is built from N separate seeds and spends only when M of them agree. With 2-of-3 you can lose one seed, or have one stolen, and still be safe. It is the standard way to remove the “one piece of paper” risk.
                    
      
                      
        
                    • Back up the descriptor too. The seeds alone are not enough: to find the money you also need the list of all the public keys (the descriptor, or the printed recovery sheet). It contains no secrets, so keep copies in several places.
                      • 
        
                    • Keep every seed in a different place, and make each one on a different day or device if you can.
                      • 
        
                    • Never reuse a seed as two of the keys, or the same seed in two different multisig wallets of the same account.
                      • 
        
                    • Test with a small amount first, and practice recovering with M of the seeds before you trust it with real savings.
                      • 
        
                    • Spending needs a wallet app (Sparrow, Nunchuk, Bitcoin Core) plus signers. VOIDFORGE only sets the wallet up; it never signs.
                      • 
      
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Method
      
                    SHA256(input string) → first 16 bytes (12 words) or 32 bytes (24 words) → BIP39 mnemonic + checksum
                    
      
                    
        
                    WordsDice rolls (1–6)Coin flips (1/0)
                    
        
                    1250128
                    
        
                    2499256
                    
      
                    
      
                    The roll or flip string is hashed as plain text. Dice are digits 1–6; coin flips are the characters 1 and 0 (choose which side counts as 1 and keep the exact string). This is the same method SeedSigner uses for its 12/24-word dice seeds (and in its coin-flip code), and VOIDFORGE reproduces SeedSigner’s published dice examples. Coldcard uses the same dice method (SHA-256 of the roll digits as plain text; 24 words, or the first half of the hash for 12), and VOIDFORGE reproduces the worked example in Coldcard’s documentation: the rolls 123456 give mirror reject rookie … garment (24 words). That example is too short to be safe; it only proves the method matches. Only 12- and 24-word seeds are generated, so every seed can be reproduced by SeedSigner-style tools. The VERIFY box still accepts 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24-word phrases from other tools.
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Master fingerprint & first address
      
                    PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(mnemonic, "mnemonic"+passphrase, 2048) → seed
                    
         HMAC-SHA512("Bitcoin seed", seed) → master private key
                    
         secp256k1 pubkey → RIPEMD160(SHA256(pubkey)) → first 4 bytes
                    
      
                    Fingerprint picture. Next to the master fingerprint is a small colored picture (a LifeHash, version 2, made from SHA-256 of the fingerprint). Sparrow Wallet shows the same picture for the same fingerprint, so a matching picture is a quick visual sign that you are looking at the same wallet. It is only a convenience: the 8-character fingerprint and the first address are the real checks, and the picture does not depend on your keys beyond the fingerprint.
                    
      
                    Watch-only export. After FORGE, the box “Watch-only wallet” shows the public key of the account m/84’/0’/0’ as a zpub (Electrum, Blue Wallet, Sparrow) and as output descriptors wpkh([fingerprint/84h/0h/0h]xpub…/0/*) for receiving and /1/* for change, with the descriptor checksum (Sparrow, Nunchuk, Bitcoin Core). The Network menu switches to testnet (test coins only; keys start with tpub, upub or vpub). The two Multisig cosigner choices give the BIP48 key (Zpub or Ypub) plus its origin, to add as one cosigner in a multisig wallet. The Address type menu switches it to Taproot (tr, BIP86), Nested SegWit (sh(wpkh), BIP49, ypub) or Legacy (pkh, BIP44), and the Account box changes the account number (almost always 0). It holds no private keys and cannot spend, but whoever has it can see every address and balance of that wallet, so give it only to your own wallet app. It is specific to the passphrase you entered. The SHOW QR buttons draw the same data as a QR code on screen so another device can scan it (many apps accept a scanned zpub or descriptor; if yours does not, use COPY). After importing, check that the app’s first receive address equals the First receive address shown here.
                    
      
                    First receive address. Also shown is the first Bitcoin mainnet receive address of a standard native SegWit (BIP84) wallet: BIP32 child keys along m/84’/0’/0’/0/0, then RIPEMD160(SHA256(pubkey)) encoded as a bc1q… bech32 address. Use it to cross-check against a wallet that imports the same words (a watch-only wallet is enough): the fingerprint alone is a weak check, a matching first address is a strong one. It is only correct for wallets that use the BIP84 path; other wallet types (legacy, nested SegWit, Taproot) show different addresses. It includes the passphrase if you entered one; VERIFY shows it without a passphrase and, if you type one into its own passphrase box, with it too.
                    
      
                    RIPEMD-160 and secp256k1 are implemented in this file (no libraries). The curve code is not constant-time, which is fine offline but another reason never to run this on a networked or shared computer. The fingerprint includes the optional BIP39 passphrase; VERIFY shows it without a passphrase and, if you type one into its own passphrase box, with it too.
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      What SELF-TEST checks
      
                    It runs automatically every time the page loads; if any test fails, seed generation is disabled and a red banner appears. Press SELF-TEST to see the full list. It checks: the BIP39 wordlist hash; official BIP39 entropy vectors (12 to 24 words); SeedSigner’s published 50- and 99-roll dice examples and 50-roll fingerprint; coin-flip vectors from an independent reference implementation of SeedSigner’s method; the abandon…about fingerprints (with and without the TREZOR passphrase); BIP32 test vector 1; the first receive address (the published BIP84 vector, a second vector from two independent libraries, and the BIP173 bech32 example); the watch-only zpub (published BIP84 vector and an independent-library vector), the descriptor checksum, a QR code matrix checked against an independent QR library, and the fingerprint picture checked against independent LifeHash code and Sparrow Wallet; passphrase normalization; RIPEMD-160 vectors; the phrase checker; and, added since, Keystone dice rules, the dice passphrase, coin-flip and word-draw helpers, Electrum seeds, every address type and its account keys on mainnet and testnet, Taproot (BIP86 and the BIP350 example), multisig cosigner keys and addresses (BIP48), Silent Payment addresses (BIP352), private key versions (SLIP132), BIP85 child seeds, keys and passwords (published vectors), SeedQR and CompactSeedQR, signed messages (BIP137 and BIP322 vectors), the transaction inspector on a known PSBT, Reforge, Ed25519 signatures (RFC 8032 vectors) and the release key’s fingerprint, a playing-card seed (as Ian Coleman’s BIP39 tool makes it) and SLIP39 shares (an official test vector). If any test fails, do not use that copy for real funds.
                    
      
                    What the self-test cannot catch: it only runs known answers through this same file, so it can miss a bug on inputs it does not cover, and a tampered file could simply fake a pass. It does not replace checking the file’s SHA256 against the release, and it does not replace comparing your words and fingerprint in a second independent tool. The network tag at the top reads the browser’s online flag only; it cannot prove the machine is air-gapped.
                    
    
                    
    
                    
      Security notes
      
                      
        
                    • Only use this offline, on a computer. Never type a real seed into a phone, website or online tool; phones and file previews often will not run this page at all.
                      • 
        
                    • The randomness meter checks face counts, long runs, repeating or stepping patterns and periodic repeats. It is advisory only: it catches lazy input, not subtle bias, and cannot prove your dice or coin are good. If it flags a pattern, FORGE SEED asks before continuing.
                      • 
        
                    • A Content-Security-Policy built into this file tells the browser to block all network access, as a second line of defense. It does not replace using an offline computer.
                      • 
        
                    • This page contains no links, and switching between dice and coin clears the entered rolls (after asking).
                      • 
        
                    • The red “WARNING: this computer looks ONLINE” banner is a hint from the browser, not proof. A machine can be connected without the browser knowing, so physically disconnect it.
                      • 
        
                    • Text boxes turn off spellcheck, autofill and autocorrect so the browser doesn’t keep what you type. The passphrase is masked, and is never shown with, copied with, printed with or saved with the words.
                      • 
        
                    • There is deliberately no "copy seed" button. SEND TO CHECK moves the words to the VERIFY box without the clipboard, but that only re-runs the same code. For a real check, write the words down by hand and type them into a second tool. The clipboard is where seeds most often leak. PRINT SEED and DOWNLOAD ask for confirmation because the print spooler and your disk can retain the seed.
                      • 
        
                    • DOWNLOAD FOR USB saves a clean copy of this page and never includes a generated seed. It is re-serialized by the browser, so its file hash will not match the original; to verify a hash, copy the original file instead. DOWNLOAD (seed) writes your seed and rolls to a plain-text file, so only use it on a trusted offline machine.
                      • 
        
                    • VOIDFORGE has not been independently audited. This software is provided “as is”, without warranty of any kind (MIT license), and the author is not liable for any loss. You alone are responsible for your funds, your backups and how you use it. If you lose the words or the passphrase, nobody can recover the funds. Before trusting it, check the release hash, use an offline computer, restore the wallet from your written backup in a second tool, and move a small amount first. It is not financial, legal or security advice.

                    VOIDFORGE v2.9.0
                    
    
                    SHA-256 of your rolls → BIP39Same method as SeedSigner and Coldcardgitlab.com/random21m/voidforge
                    
  
                    

                    

                    

                    

                    CAMERA ON
                    

                    

                    Before you make real keys
                    

                    VOIDFORGE is an educational tool. It works fully offline and never stores your rolls, words or keys, and its code is open to read, but it has not been independently audited. Your computer, though, can keep secrets. Three things worth knowing first:
                    

                    1
                    Your computer may keep a copy of your keys. It can write memory to the hard drive (swap files, hibernation) without asking, and the browser cannot stop it.What to do: for real money, use an offline computer with an encrypted drive, and turn hibernation off.
                    

                    2
                    Copying can leak. Clipboard history can keep what you copy or paste, and may sync it to your other devices.What to do: write seeds on paper; avoid copy and paste for anything secret, and turn clipboard history off.
                    

                    3
                    Keys can stay in memory after you finish. Wiping the page is a precaution, not a guarantee.What to do: when you are done, close the browser and restart the computer.
                    

                    


                    Practicing with a test seed? Nothing here applies. For real money, start with a small amount. Offline, this shows once in each browser tab; online, every time the page opens. END SESSION in the MENU wipes the page and shows it again.
